raw_case_text: A 44-year-old male presented with sudden onset, diminution of vision in both eyes for 10 days. He gave history of fever, myalgia, and weakness one week prior to onset of ocular problem. He was previously healthy, not known to have diabetes mellitus or hypertension. There was no relevant family or social history of medical significance. During clinical evaluation and laboratory investigation for fever; typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular disease and bleeding disorders were absent. He was diagnosed to have dengue fever as NS1 antigen and IgM antibody were positive. After conservative management, his platelet count had improved from 49x103/microL to 176x103/microL (normal range, 150-450x103/microL) over a week period. At presentation, his best-corrected visual acuity was 1/60 in the right eye (OD) and 6/18 in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment findings were normal. Fundus examination revealed vitritis, perivascular exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, macular edema, peripapillary retinal whitening, and cotton wool spots in both eyes, with additional retinal whitening affecting the right macula (Figure 1). Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed disc and perivascular leakage limited to posterior pole along with patches of blocked fluorescence. In addition, there was capillary nonperfusion due to occlusion of multiple small arterioles supplying the macula of the right eye confirming macular ischemia (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography of both eyes demonstrated macular edema with subretinal fluid. A diagnosis of bilateral retinal vasculitis with right eye macular infarction was made. Echocardiography and carotid Doppler studies revealed normal cardiac and carotid artery status. The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone which was futile even after three days of treatment. Then he was counseled for treatment with immunoglobulin, which the patient refused and left for a second opinion without returning back to us.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old male presenting with sudden-onset diminution of vision in both eyes for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 44-year-old male developed fever, myalgia, and weakness lasting approximately one week, managed conservatively with resolution of systemic symptoms. One week after the onset of systemic symptoms, he experienced sudden-onset bilateral visual impairment progressing over 10 days, prompting ophthalmologic evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, bleeding disorders, or collagen vascular diseases. Family and social history non-contributory.
subjective.review_of_systems: Weakness and myalgia preceding visual symptoms; no focal neurologic or cardiopulmonary complaints at ocular presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmologic examination: Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) 1/60 in the right eye (OD) and 6/18 in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment examination normal bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination: Bilateral vitritis, perivascular exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, macular edema, peripapillary retinal whitening, and cotton wool spots in both eyes, with additional retinal whitening affecting the right macula.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: Nadir of 49 x 10^3/microL during febrile phase, improving to 176 x 10^3/microL (reference range: 150-450 x 10^3/microL) within one week. Diagnostic testing negative for typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular diseases, and coagulopathies. Transthoracic echocardiography and carotid Doppler ultrasound: Normal cardiac valves, function, and carotid arterial status.
objective.advanced_workup: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA): Disc and perivascular leakage limited to the posterior pole with patches of blocked fluorescence bilaterally; capillary nonperfusion secondary to occlusion of multiple small arterioles supplying the right macula, confirming macular ischemia/infarction. Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Bilateral macular edema with subretinal fluid accumulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection complicated by bilateral retinal vasculitis, bilateral macular edema, and right-sided macular branch retinal arteriolar occlusion/infarction. Dengue confirmation established by positive Dengue NS1 antigen and Dengue IgM antibody during the acute febrile illness. Typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular diseases, and cardiac/carotid embolic sources were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy for 3 days without functional visual improvement. Immunoglobulin therapy was recommended; however, the patient declined further intervention and discharged against medical advice to seek a second opinion.
